name: Louis XIV
summary: Louis XIV ruled France as an absolute monarch who held that kings act in God's place and have free disposal of their subjects' goods for the state's needs. He subdued the Parlements and nobility, promoted state-run mercantilist industry through Colbert, fought wars of expansion, enforced Catholic uniformity (revoking the Edict of Nantes in 1685, issuing the Code Noir) and upheld Gallican limits on papal power. Near death he advised his heir to keep peace, ease taxes and fear God.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Forbade trade in foreign luxury goods, set up state-backed manufactures 'par autorité' and arrested merchants' stock; his government directed the economy rather than leaving it to markets.

property-fundamental.rationale: Told the Dauphin that kings are absolute lords with full and free disposal of all property, of the church as of laymen, to use according to the state's general need.

strong-leader.rationale: Wrote that on important matters the sovereign should decide by his own judgment after hearing counsel; he personally subdued the Parlement so that it stopped debating edicts verified in his presence, and described the result as the 'parfait rétablissement de l'autorité royale'.

state-harmful.rationale: Wrote of the state's grandeur and good as the king's overriding duty and built an expanded state apparatus; the idea that the state is unnecessary is the opposite of his stated views.

empower-police-military.rationale: Expanded the army and his household troops, instituted strict inspection, and reformed Paris policing through a dedicated council that reported to him.

decide-locally.rationale: Centralised government: took personal control of appointments, justice and the military, subordinated provincial parlements and the nobility, and sent special commissions (Grands Jours) to the provinces.

more-religion-public.rationale: Told Philip V to make God honoured wherever he had power and to give the example; his Mémoires describe steps taken to advance religion, and he revoked the Edict of Nantes to impose Catholic uniformity.

free-trade.rationale: His Mémoires treat imports of foreign goods as a loss to France and prohibit them to protect French manufactures.

nation-first.rationale: Wrote that the interest of the state must come first and that a prince should build his designs on knowledge of his own forces rather than on others' promises.

revolution-justified.rationale: Describes rebels and the leaders of revolt (including his own Fronde-era opponents) as guilty of disobedience who end badly; he praised the army's loyalty that made rebel subjects return to obedience.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Banned trade in foreign textiles to protect new French manufactures, and his government revised tariffs protectively (Colbert); he also asked Turenne about reciprocal duties on French ships.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Wrote that he established silk, cloth, glass and crystal manufactures in the kingdom with state money and authority so that sums leaving France would be kept at home.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: His Mémoires for the Dauphin defend hereditary monarchy as the best government, comparing it favourably with republics and aristocratic states, and he describes kingship as a 'grand, noble et délicieux' office (Réflexions sur le métier de roi).

democracy-best.rationale: Inferred: he judged states governed by the suffrages of many to be less honourable and trustworthy than monarchies.

direct-votes.rationale: Inferred: he held that republics and assemblies governed by many suffrages act on interest alone and that subjects should obey; no role for popular votes.

right-to-secede.rationale: Treated regions in revolt as 'sujets rebelles' who must return to obedience; no recorded support for secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Wrote that princes bred in the brilliance of birth and honourable education have noble and generous sentiments, whereas men of middling condition governing aristocratic states act only from interest.

separate-church-state.rationale: Revoked toleration to establish Catholicism alone, closed Protestant worship, made the Code Noir enforce Catholic discipline in the colonies and advised his grandson to promote religion with royal power.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Centralised justice in the crown, reformed civil procedure by ordinance and took personal command of the standing army; the Grands Jours punished lords' private violence.

military-superiority.rationale: His Mémoires describe enlarging the army, strict inspection and discipline, and fortifying frontiers to dominate his rivals; he fought wars for decades to hold Europe's greatest army.

taxation-theft.rationale: Held that the king may dispose of subjects' goods for the state's need and imposed taxation; in 1709 he described extraordinary levies as necessary for the state's glory and safety.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Mixed: he expanded France by the Devolution War, Franco-Dutch War and Réunions and boasted of having extended the empire's limits; but on his deathbed he reportedly told Louis XV 'J'ai trop aimé la guerre: ne m'imitez pas'.

single-common-good.rationale: Repeatedly wrote that the interest of the state comes first ('tout rapporter au bien de l'État') and that the king alone, using prudence, discerns the good among competing claims; he rejected divide-and-rule between factions.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Urged Philip V in 1700 to restore his finances, and on his deathbed told Louis XV not to imitate his excessive spending; Colbert turned deficit into surplus by 1666.

rule-by-example.rationale: Mixed: told Philip V to promote virtue by example, and stressed the influence of a prince's honourable conduct, yet also relied on exemplary punishments and repression.

national-self-determination.rationale: Annexed Flanders, Franche-Comté and Alsace through dynastic claims and the Chambers of Reunion, and prepared an 'Abrégé des droits du roi sur plusieurs royaumes', rather than recognising nations' own wishes.

ban-interest.rationale: His government cut the legal rate of interest from 1/18 to 1/20 so that borrowers could get money on better terms, treating lending at interest as lawful.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Directed manufactures, trade, the church's discipline and justice reform through the state; he did not limit government to defence, justice and property protection.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Issued the Code Noir, which treats enslaved people as property with different punishments and legal capacity, and a rank-based law that withheld rights from Protestants.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Grounded sovereignty in 'les lois de l'État et les droits du sang' and in God's place, and condemned subjects who rebelled against the sovereign so given; he never treated subjects' consent as the basis of legitimacy.

trade-surplus.rationale: Explained that the large sums spent on foreign goods 'étoient autant de perdu pour la France' and set up manufactures to keep twelve million a year in the kingdom, a mercantilist export-over-import aim.

population-transfer.rationale: The Edict of Fontainebleau ordered pastors who refused conversion to leave within fifteen days, and the Code Noir ordered Jews expelled from the colonies within three months as 'ennemis déclarés du nom chrétien'.

separated-powers.rationale: Stressed deciding matters himself ('le seul qui fais marcher la chose'), subjected the Parlement completely and treated council advice as his to override; he saw no value in rival power centres.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Personally appointed officers down to minor posts, directed his campaigns, chose his ministers himself (e.g. Pomponne), and advised Philip V to lead his armies in person.

people-in-arms.rationale: Replaced noble levies with a disciplined professional army under his direct control and insisted on 'obéissance ponctuelle'.

death-penalty.rationale: Code Noir provisions he issued prescribe death for repeated escape and striking a master; the Grands Jours severely punished abusive nobles; the statement is about gravest crimes such as terrorism, which his record fits only loosely.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Revoked the Edict of Nantes' guarantees and banned Protestant worship, refusing any exemption for minority religious practice.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Argued that royal disposal of private and clerical property is justified by 'le besoin général de leur État' and that clergy should not be exempt from public burdens.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Mixed record: he extended the régale, had the clergy adopt the 1682 Gallican Articles, banned new monasteries and capped monks' numbers, and held kings to have disposal of church property; yet he gave the church privileges and refused to touch its spiritual jurisdiction.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Described the king's office as 'une fonction toute divine' held in God's place, which supports sacredness, but he never claimed divine descent, so the statement is only partly matched.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Wrote that kings are 'seigneurs absolus' with free disposal of all property, and that 'rien que la justice et la raison n'a de pouvoir sur moi' (1667); he forbade the Parlement to discuss edicts he had verified in person.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Inferred: he preferred rule by one over aristocratic and republican states and praised the monarch's independence of both.

leader-cult.rationale: Mixed: he cultivated royal glory and 'fonction toute divine', but declined the Parlement's congratulatory harangues for his conquests as premature.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Mixed: he barred foreign textiles and applied mercantilist rules to colonies, but also sought reciprocal trade with England and Holland rather than total closure.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Kept and fixed ranks and orders (a règlement of ranks among troops, honours for 'gens de qualité'); his Mémoires treat birth and breeding as a source of noble sentiment.

elective-rulers.rationale: Treated the throne as passing by 'les droits du sang' under the laws of the state; his own manoeuvres to buy Polish electors were for placing a prince of his house, not endorsing choice by the political nation.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Condemned the chief of any revolt as having given 'un exemple de désobéissance envers celui que les lois de l'État et les droits du sang lui avoient donné pour souverain', and counselled upholding authority against cabal and sedition.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Records that he ordered the Parlement of Paris to stop discussing edicts verified in his presence, to demonstrate its 'entier assujétissement', and viewed provincial parlements' compliance as proof of restored royal authority; Code Louis (1667) limited remonstrances.

native-born-offices.rationale: Advised Philip V that viceroys and governors in Spain should always be Spaniards and not to favour French servants against Spaniards.

office-by-exam.rationale: Chose officers and ministers himself ('je me donnois le soin de distribuer moi-même jusques aux moindres charges') and issued an edict moderating the price of purchased offices.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Claimed full royal disposal of the goods of clergy and laity for the state's needs and imposed taxes by edict, forbidding Parlement to debate them; in 1709 he asked the nation for help only as a request.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Mémoires note his 'intelligence avec les mécontens d'Angleterre' and encouragement of Portugal's war against Spain; the record of material support to insurgents is partial.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Stated that public affairs depend on general subordination and that rulers should always uphold the authority of those who command against cabal and sedition.

non-intervention.rationale: His Mémoires record paying subsidies and pensions to foreign nobles, intriguing in Poland and England and funding Denmark to influence other states' affairs.

religious-nation.rationale: His religious policy aimed at one faith for the whole kingdom: the Edict declared most Protestants already converted and ordered the rest to conform or leave the public sphere.

suppress-opposition.rationale: His Mémoires record using the 1666 Grands Jours and the Parlement's submission as examples; he sought the 'extirpation' of Jansenism, banned Huguenot worship and treated factions and cabals as sedition to be put down.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Edict of Fontainebleau (1685) banned all Protestant worship on pain of the galleys and confiscation; the Code Noir (art. 3 in the Wikipedia summary) barred public practice of any religion but Catholicism.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Colonial policy under his reign applied mercantilism, seeking maximum benefit for the homeland; the Code Noir he issued regulates the colonies from France.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Told the Dauphin that rulers, 'tenant la place de Dieu', share in God's knowledge and authority, and called kingship 'une fonction toute divine'; he told Philip V and Louis XV that they owed everything to God.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Built and expanded a large standing army and navy.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Instructed his son and grandson as heirs, pressed his house's claims (Spanish succession, Philip V) and at death handed the throne to his great-grandson Louis XV.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Mixed: he issued the 1667 civil ordinance as a general code through a drafting conference, but also decided matters personally and reserved the right to override.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: he attacked 'rois sans religion' and promoted Catholic uniformity in all schools and institutions, so would reject state promotion of atheism.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Points both ways: he began several wars of conquest, but advised Philip V in 1700 to fight only when forced and told Louis XV in 1715 to keep peace and not imitate his love of war.

open-diplomacy.rationale: His Mémoires record secret treaty articles, a secret treaty with Denmark and a secret promise to Charles II; the Secret Treaty of Dover (1670) was kept hidden.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Wrote that in war authority must be absolute and obedience exact, and that quarrels over command are dangerous.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Revoked the Edict of Nantes, ended recognition of Protestant worship and sought the extirpation of Jansenism; only the royal-approved Catholic doctrine had legal standing.

national-church-status.rationale: Treated Catholicism as the kingdom's sole religion and the Gallican Church as the crown's own; he made the 1682 Gallican Declaration law and required its teaching.

no-business-privileges.rationale: His government gave favoured manufacturers and monopoly companies state privileges and forbade competing imports.

notes: Louis XIV's Mémoires were drafted with secretaries under his direction and count as his words. The deathbed advice to Louis XV is secondhand. The Code Noir was drafted by Colbert and Seignelay on his order and issued in his name; answers drawn from it rely on that record rather than on any personal statement. The remark 'L'État, c'est moi' is apocryphal and was not used. His views on war shifted late in life (advice of 1700 and 1715 urging peace).
